title: Gameweek 6 Captaincy Matrix: the armband, the differentials, and the bench calls
dek: Gibbs-White leads the captaincy matrix for Gameweek 6, away at CRY. The differentials, the hard fixtures, and the players whose minutes are not safe.
body:
## The armband is the biggest call you make

Captaincy doubles a score, which makes it worth more than most transfers. A ten-point swing between two obvious picks is routine; over a season the armband decides more rank than any single buy.

:::takeaways
- **Gibbs-White** is the safe pick: 16% owned, away at CRY.
- **E.Le Fée** is the differential at 3.5% ownership.
- Last round the field captained **Haaland**.
:::

**Gibbs-White** travels to CRY at a difficulty of 3. At 16% ownership the armband on him is close to a non-decision: captaining the same player as most of the field neither gains nor loses rank, which is exactly why it is the correct default unless you have a reason to move.

## The differential armband

Captaining off-template is a leveraged bet: it wins more rank than it should when it lands and costs more than it should when it does not. These are the players with a kind fixture and an ownership low enough to make the bet worth taking.

| Player | Team | Price | Opponent | Proj. pts | Owned | FDR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **E.Le Fée** | SUN | £5.8m | BHA (H) | 4.1 | 3.5% | {fdr:2} |
| **King** | FUL | £5.5m | IPS (A) | 3.9 | 2% | {fdr:2} |

| **Gonzalo** | FUL | £6.0m | IPS (A) | 3.8 | 3.6% | {fdr:2} |
| **Barry** | EVE | £5.6m | HUL (A) | 3.6 | 7.9% | {fdr:2} |
| **Enciso** | IPS | £5.5m | FUL (H) | 3.4 | 0.8% | {fdr:2} |

:::callout warning
Effective ownership — the figure that actually decides whether a captaincy gains you rank — depends on how many managers captain a player, not just how many own him. FPL does not publish that number, and nothing on this page estimates it. The ownership column above is ownership. Treat the gap between the two as unknown rather than small.
:::

## The defences they are up against

A captaincy pick is half about the player and half about who he is playing. FPL publishes its own defensive rating for every team, home and away separately, and it is the one piece of opponent information that does not need a season's worth of results behind it.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

### Gibbs-White — NFO, £8.0m

16% of the field own him. He travels to CRY, whose home defence is average. He projects 5.4 points for this fixture, against a season average of 5.2 a gameweek on 2.58 expected involvements.

### Haaland — MCI, £15.6m

73.3% of the field own him. He travels to LIV, whose home defence is average. He projects 5.2 points for this fixture, against a season average of 6.6 a gameweek on 3.84 expected involvements.

### B.Fernandes — MUN, £12.0m

40% of the field own him. He hosts TOT, whose away defence is average. He projects 5.2 points for this fixture, against a season average of 5.8 a gameweek on 3.41 expected involvements.

### Mbeumo — MUN, £7.9m

21.5% of the field own him. He hosts TOT, whose away defence is average. He projects 5.1 points for this fixture, against a season average of 4.6 a gameweek on 3.35 expected involvements.

## What the field did last time

The most-captained player in Gameweek 4 was **Haaland**, and he returned 9 — 18 with the armband on.

The best available return was **Groß** on 17, so the difference between the crowd's armband and the optimal one was 16 points. Chasing the optimal captain every week is not a strategy — nobody hits it — but the size of that gap is why the decision deserves more thought than it usually gets.

## The vice-captaincy

The vice only pays out when your captain does not play, which makes it a decision most managers make carelessly and then regret twice a season. The rule that matters: your vice should kick off **after** your captain wherever possible, so that a captain benched at the last minute can still be covered — and he should never be a rotation risk himself, because a captain who does not play backed by a vice who also does not play is a guaranteed zero on a doubled slot.

**B.Fernandes** (40% owned, home to TOT) is the natural cover here.

## Three ways this goes wrong

- **Captaining form into a wall.** A player in good touch against a strong defence away from home is a worse bet than an average player at home to a poor one. Form is a weaker signal than the fixture, and it is the one that feels more compelling.
- **Chasing last week.** The player who returned fifteen last gameweek is not more likely to return this one, but he is more likely to be captained. That is the mechanism by which the field collectively buys high.
- **Going differential for its own sake.** An off-template armband should be justified by the fixture, not by the ownership. If the only argument for a captain is that few people own him, that is an argument for a lottery ticket.

## The bench dilemma

Starting eleven decisions are quieter than captaincy and cost nearly as much. Two categories are worth a second look before the deadline: players with a genuinely hard fixture, and players whose minutes have not been reliable.
